prompt: Besides encrypting the connection, what does TLS prove?
hint: Encryption to an impostor is worthless.

choices.text: That the site is honest and safe to buy from
choices.why: A certificate says nothing about honesty.

choices.text: That the server holds the name
choices.why: Right. The other half of the job.

choices.text: That the page has no malware
choices.why: Nobody inspects the content before signing.

choices.text: That the company behind it is registered with the government
choices.why: A domain-validated certificate checks control of the name only.

prompt: Which field of a certificate do browsers check the requested name against?
hint: Not the older one.

choices.text: The Common Name field
choices.why: Browsers no longer rely on it.

choices.text: The Issuer field
choices.why: That names who signed, not who it is for.

choices.text: Subject Alternative Name
choices.why: Right. It listed both bookshop names.

choices.text: The certificate's serial number
choices.why: The serial identifies the certificate, not the site.

prompt: Why does a server not send the root certificate in its chain?
hint: What would a root the client does not already hold prove?

choices.text: A root it does not already trust proves nothing
choices.why: Right. Anybody can make a self-signed certificate.

choices.text: Roots are too large to send over a handshake
choices.why: Size is not the reason.

choices.text: Roots are secret and must never be shared
choices.why: A root certificate is public; its private key is what stays secret.

choices.text: TLS 1.3 forbids it
choices.why: No version forbids it; it is simply useless.

prompt: A phishing site at `ipe-livros-promo.example` shows a valid padlock. What does that padlock establish?
hint: What did the CA check?

choices.text: That Ipê Livros approved the site
choices.why: Nobody asked Ipê Livros anything.

choices.text: Nothing, because a phishing site cannot obtain a certificate
choices.why: It can, for the name it controls.

choices.text: That the connection reaches whoever controls that look-alike name
choices.why: Right. Precise, and narrower than people think.

choices.text: That the site was scanned for fraud
choices.why: Domain validation checks the name only.

prompt: In a self-signed certificate, what is the issuer?
hint: Look at the `openssl x509` output.

choices.text: The same name as the subject
choices.why: Right. It vouched for itself.

choices.text: Let's Encrypt
choices.why: No CA was involved.

choices.text: The operating system's root store
choices.why: That store was never consulted when it was made.

choices.text: openssl itself, as a built-in authority
choices.why: openssl is a tool, not an authority.

prompt: What does `curl -k` against the self-signed site actually prove?
hint: -k switches the check off.

choices.text: That the certificate is valid
choices.why: It was never checked.

choices.text: That the right server answered
choices.why: Without the check, anybody could have answered.

choices.text: That the private key is safe
choices.why: Nothing about the key's safety is tested by a client.

choices.text: Nothing about who answered
choices.why: Right. Encrypted, to whoever was there.

prompt: Two of your own servers talk over a private network, and you control both. When is a self-signed certificate acceptable there?
hint: The client must have a copy it can believe.

choices.text: Never, under any circumstances
choices.why: This is exactly its legitimate case.

choices.text: When the client trusts it with --cacert
choices.why: Right. You copied it there yourself.

choices.text: When the client skips verification with -k
choices.why: -k trusts anything, which is no trust at all.

choices.text: Only if it is valid for more than a full year
choices.why: Validity length has nothing to do with trust.

prompt: Match each ACME challenge to what it needs.
hint: The lesson's table.

pairs.right: an API to change the domain's DNS
port 443 and a server that speaks it

prompt: A company wants a certificate for `*.intra.example` on servers nobody outside can reach. Which challenge?
hint: Wildcard, and no inbound access.

choices.text: HTTP-01
choices.why: It needs port 80 reachable, and cannot issue a wildcard.

choices.text: TLS-ALPN-01
choices.why: It needs 443 reachable, and cannot issue a wildcard either.

choices.text: DNS-01
choices.why: Right. The only one for wildcards and unreachable machines.

choices.text: None; such names cannot get certificates
choices.why: DNS-01 does exactly this.

prompt: Put the steps of an ACME order in order.
hint: Account first, certificate last.
items: Place an order for the names
Receive and meet a challenge per name
Send a CSR and download the certificate
trap: The CSR comes after validation, not before.

prompt: Why can't the VM you built in lesson 1 get a certificate from Let's Encrypt?
hint: Where does Let's Encrypt check from?

choices.text: Let's Encrypt refuses virtual machines
choices.why: It cannot even tell.

choices.text: Its names exist only on the VM
choices.why: Right. The system working as intended.

choices.text: Ubuntu blocks ACME traffic by default
choices.why: Nothing in Ubuntu does that.

choices.text: certbot only works with Pebble servers
choices.why: It works with any ACME server.

prompt: Why does the lab set `"httpPort": 80` in Pebble's configuration?
hint: Pebble's default is 5002.

choices.text: Port 5002 is reserved by the system
choices.why: It is not; Pebble picked it to avoid needing root.

choices.text: So challenges are checked on Nginx's port
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: To serve Pebble's own API on that port
choices.why: The API is on 14000.

choices.text: To redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS for the site
choices.why: That is Nginx's job, not Pebble's.

prompt: `certificateValidityPeriod` was 7776000 seconds. How many days is that?
hint: 86400 seconds a day.

prompt: Pebble's root is called `Pebble Root CA` followed by a different number after every start. What follows from that?
hint: A new root, every time.

choices.text: Old trust in its root stops counting
choices.why: Right. You would fetch and trust the new one.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since roots are interchangeable
choices.why: A different root means a different key.

choices.text: The number is the root's expiry date
choices.why: It is random.

choices.text: Let's Encrypt changes its roots the same way
choices.why: Let's Encrypt's roots last for years and ship with every system.

prompt: Which file should Nginx's `ssl_certificate` point at?
hint: The site and its intermediate.

choices.text: `cert.pem`
choices.why: Without the intermediate, clients that have not cached it fail.

choices.text: `chain.pem`
choices.why: That is the intermediate alone.

choices.text: `privkey.pem`
choices.why: That goes in ssl_certificate_key.

choices.text: `fullchain.pem`
choices.why: Right.

prompt: How did certbot's webroot method prove control of ipelivros.example?
hint: Nginx's access log has the evidence.

choices.text: It stopped Nginx and listened on port 80
choices.why: That is the standalone method; Nginx never stopped.

choices.text: Nginx served a token file it wrote
choices.why: Right. The VA fetched it over HTTP.

choices.text: It edited a DNS record for the domain
choices.why: That is DNS-01.

choices.text: It sent the private key to the CA
choices.why: The private key never leaves the server.

prompt: A site works in your browser and fails in `curl` with "unable to get local issuer certificate". What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Your browser may have cached something.

choices.text: The intermediate is missing from the chain
choices.why: Right. Use fullchain.pem.

choices.text: curl does not support TLS 1.3 yet
choices.why: It does; and this message is about the chain.

choices.text: The certificate expired last night at midnight
choices.why: The browser would have failed too.

choices.text: The name is missing from /etc/hosts
choices.why: Then curl would not connect at all.

prompt: After `update-ca-certificates`, curl reported `ssl_verify_result` 0. What does 0 mean?
hint: Zero is success, as with exit codes.

choices.text: The chain was checked and accepted
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Verification was skipped
choices.why: Nothing skipped it; there was no -k.

choices.text: Zero certificates were sent
choices.why: Two were sent.

choices.text: The session was resumed
choices.why: That is a different field.

prompt: Why does the port-80 server block keep `location /.well-known/acme-challenge/` instead of redirecting everything?
hint: Think ninety days ahead.

choices.text: Browsers cannot follow redirects to HTTPS
choices.why: They follow them every day.

choices.text: It makes the site faster to load
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Renewals check it over port 80
choices.why: Right. A swallowed challenge fails the next renewal.

choices.text: Certbot's files are not allowed under HTTPS
choices.why: There is no such rule.

prompt: The handshake test with `-tls1_1` got `alert protocol version`. Who refused?
hint: The client was told to offer 1.1.

choices.text: The client, as OpenSSL does by default
choices.why: The client was made to offer it; the alert came back from the server.

choices.text: Pebble
choices.why: Pebble is not in this connection.

choices.text: The kernel
choices.why: The kernel knows nothing of TLS versions.

choices.text: Nginx, because of `ssl_protocols`
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Nginx's TLS session cache is written `ssl_session_cache ___:TLS:10m;` so every worker uses the same one.
hint: The same reason as an upstream's zone.

prompt: By default, certbot renews a certificate when it has how many days or fewer left?
hint: The commented line at the top of the renewal file.

prompt: certbot renews the files, and Nginx keeps serving the old certificate. What is missing?
hint: Nginx reads certificates when it loads its configuration.

choices.text: A deploy hook that reloads Nginx
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A cron job that restarts the whole machine every night
choices.why: A reload is enough, and costs nothing.

choices.text: Pointing Nginx at archive/ instead of live/
choices.why: archive/ paths change on every renewal; live/ is the stable one.

choices.text: A longer validity period from the CA
choices.why: It would only delay the same problem.

prompt: Why did the lab's `certbot renew --dry-run` need `--server`?
hint: Which server does --dry-run use by default?

choices.text: Dry runs are not allowed against Pebble
choices.why: The run against Pebble succeeded.

choices.text: The renewal file no longer named any server
choices.why: It said `server = https://localhost:14000/dir`.

choices.text: Dry runs default to Let's Encrypt staging
choices.why: Right. On a real server, leave it out.

choices.text: To skip certbot's random sleep before renewing
choices.why: That is `--no-random-sleep-on-renew`.

prompt: Your monitoring reads the expiry date from `/etc/letsencrypt/live/.../cert.pem` and says 60 days left, while visitors see an expired certificate. What is wrong with the check?
hint: Which certificate do visitors receive?

choices.text: It reads the file, not what the server actually sends
choices.why: Right. Nginx was never reloaded after the renewal.

choices.text: 60 days is too short a threshold
choices.why: The threshold is not the problem; the source of the date is.

choices.text: openssl miscalculates dates in another time zone
choices.why: Certificate dates are in GMT and compared correctly.

choices.text: The certificate on disk is the intermediate
choices.why: cert.pem is the site's own certificate.

prompt: What did Caddy need, beyond the site block, to obtain certificates in this lab?
hint: Two global options a real server would leave out.

choices.text: A certbot installation and a webroot folder
choices.why: Caddy is its own ACME client.

choices.text: A port-80 redirect block in the Caddyfile
choices.why: Caddy redirects by itself.

choices.text: Pebble's address and API certificate
choices.why: Right: acme_ca and acme_ca_root.

choices.text: A deploy hook to reload after renewal
choices.why: Caddy loads its own renewals.

prompt: Caddy redirected with 308 where Nginx used 301. What does that change for a form that POSTs to the HTTP address?
hint: Which of the two keeps the method?

choices.text: Nothing; both codes behave the same
choices.why: Browsers turn a POST into a GET on a 301.

choices.text: With 308 the browser repeats the POST to HTTPS; with 301 it would become a GET and lose the body
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: 308 is temporary, so it is not cached
choices.why: 308 is permanent; 307 is the temporary one.

choices.text: 308 refuses POST entirely
choices.why: It preserves it.

prompt: Which of these would make next season's automatic renewal fail on the lesson's Nginx setup? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does an HTTP-01 renewal need?

choices.text: A firewall rule that closes port 80
choices.why: Right. The CA checks over port 80.

choices.text: Removing the acme-challenge location from the port-80 block
choices.why: Right. The token would be redirected away.

choices.text: Disabling certbot.timer
choices.why: Right. Nothing would try.

choices.text: Adding `ssl_session_cache`
choices.why: A session cache has nothing to do with issuance.

prompt: A teammate's script calls the internal API with `curl -k` "because the certificate is self-signed". What is the better fix?
hint: Keep the check, and give it something to check against.

choices.text: Keep -k, since nobody outside can reach the network
choices.why: Internal networks get compromised too, and -k hides it.

choices.text: Switch the API to plain HTTP instead
choices.why: That removes both encryption and identity.

choices.text: Trust its certificate instead, with --cacert
choices.why: Right. The check stays on.

choices.text: Make the certificate valid for ten years
choices.why: Validity length does not make a certificate trusted.
